Model-Based Agentic Software Engineering

Generative AI is shifting software engineering from a practice built around scarce implementation toward one built around abundant, low-cost code. The hard part stops being writing code and becomes governing the conditions under which fast code can be trusted. This catalogue serves a method for doing that: Model-Based Agentic Software Engineering (MAGE) — engineering with a fleet of coding agents by binding intent to typed models the fleet reasons through, and governing what it builds with mechanisms that prevent or detect drift.

MAGE is one method with two theses — a Modeling Thesis and an Alignment Thesis — and this page is built around them. Every unit below is a clickable card: open it for a quick peek, then follow the link through to the full treatment in the book. QUICK START: install the skills for Claude →

Thesis I of II The Modeling Thesis Documentation, taken to its limit, is a typed model.

Give agents good documentation and tests, then point them at it — the first move everyone finds on their own. The step the training data won't suggest is the next one: documentation has a hierarchy, and its top is not prose. It is a typed model. A context-bounded agent working on a context-exceeding system needs a typed, queryable, drift-checked model to reason through — the bridge between the agent and the codebase it cannot fit in its head. The catalogue's models-bridge role is this bridge, made concrete.

read the full treatment →
Thesis II of II The Alignment Thesis A quality goal splits into a constraint that prevents and a sensor that catches.

A mechanism the environment enforces keeps output aligned with intent, and it takes one of two forms: prevent the error, or catch it. However you arrived at the goal — up front from the domain or in response to a failure — a constraint scopes the action space so the whole class is impossible, and a sensor lets the mistake happen but detects it in time, failing the loop iteration so the agent runs again to fix it. A third set of goals splits into neither — no sensor and no constraint reaches them, so they stay a human job; that residual is what the mechanisms leave behind.

The four definitions — the vocabulary the theses ride on
DefinitionModelA useful approximation of a phenomenon (simplified, but good enough to predict)…
🔵 Model — A useful approximation of a phenomenon (simplified, but good enough to predict) — and, as this book uses it, a blueprint: a prescriptive description of a system to be built, which the built system is bound to realize.
  • The first sense — a useful approximation A simplified description prized because it predicts, not because it is exact. All models are wrong, some are useful; fidelity trades against cost, and how much fidelity you need is in the eye of the application.
  • The second sense — a blueprint A prescriptive description of the system you intend to build. A system built to a model may elaborate on it but may not diverge from it — which is what lets a model serve as an agent's marching orders.
  • Constraint, blueprint, and knowledge base at once A model handed to an agent is at once a constraint (bounding what may be built), a blueprint (saying what to build), and — because the agent reasons over it — the knowledge base for the artifact under construction.

Book home: Part 2 — Definitions (owed — drafted, not yet landed) · lexicon · projected from the definitions model.

DefinitionAgentA controllable intelligence capable of independent reasoning over a knowledge base…
🔵 Agent — A controllable intelligence capable of independent reasoning over a knowledge base.
  • On "intelligence." Given a set of constraints and a goal, it can devise a means of satisfying the goal without violating the constraints — a raven dropping pebbles to raise the water it cannot otherwise reach.
  • On "controllable" (not controlled). You can change its environment and the knowledge available to it and it does different things, generally following orders. Controllable means probabilistic guarantees; controlled means perfect ones. That one adjective is why governance is a major part of this book — if agents were controlled, we would not need governance at all.
  • On "independent reasoning." It genuinely reasons in response to a query — not merely retrieving or pattern-matching stored answers.
  • On "over a knowledge base." The thing it reasons over. For this book, the models are that knowledge base — which is what ties the agent definition to the model definition.

Book home: Part 2 — Definitions (owed — drafted, not yet landed) · lexicon · projected from the definitions model.

DefinitionEngineeringThe discipline of developing operable technological artifacts to solve problems, and of analytically identifying and assessing the competing means to those solutions, each with distinct trade-offs…
🔵 Engineering — The discipline of developing operable technological artifacts to solve problems, and of analytically identifying and assessing the competing means to those solutions, each with distinct trade-offs.
  • On "develops operable artifacts." Engineering produces something that works — a technological artifact, with human operators, that addresses a real problem.
  • On "analytical assessment of competing means." This is what separates the engineer from the technician: if you cannot articulate the trade-offs, you are not engineering. An engineer weighs competing architectures and designs against desired properties.
  • On "predictive." An engineer can model and predict the outcomes of the decisions they are about to make — from the architecture and design they propose — prior to building. Prediction-before-construction is the engineering move.

Book home: Part 2 — Definitions (owed — drafted, not yet landed) · lexicon · projected from the definitions model.

DefinitionSoftware engineeringSoftware development produces a functioning artifact…
🔵 Software engineering — Software development produces a functioning artifact. Software engineering predictively selects a software artifact according to its desired properties.
  • Development vs. engineering. Development asks "does it function and meet requirements?" Engineering asks "of the artifacts that would function, which one should we build, given the properties we want?" — and answers before building it.
  • Why the book is about software engineering. Prediction-before-construction, applied to software: choosing the artifact whose properties best serve the goal, not merely one that runs.

Book home: Part 2 — Definitions (owed — drafted, not yet landed) · lexicon · projected from the definitions model.

Two schools, and the midway between them
Between two schoolsVibe codingall velocity — no durable guardrails

Prompt an agent, accept what looks right, iterate by feel. Fast and fluid, but quality rests on the model and your eye. At scale the same failures keep recurring, and human review becomes the bottleneck.

Examples:
  • Karpathy — coined “vibe coding”
  • Steve Yegge’s Gas Town
all velocity — no durable guardrailsread the full treatment →
The midwayGovernance-centricvelocity + guardrails grown from failure

The midway. Velocity exposes failures; you convert each recurring one into a guardrail: a type, a lint, a gate. The guardrails grow out of real failures, so code stays fast and stays trustworthy.

velocity + guardrails grown from failureread the full treatment →
Between two schoolsOversight-centricall oversight — everything checked

Check everything before you trust it, whether a human reviews every change or a formal specification is verified against. Rigorous and safe, but checking becomes the bottleneck: all of it must be vetted, and neither humans nor specs anticipate the failures that only appear at velocity. (Spec-driven development is this, with the spec as the checker.)

Examples:
  • Meyer, CACM — “From Probable to Provable”
  • vibe-OS / vibe-tools (formal tooling for AI)
all oversight — everything checkedread the full treatment →
The spectrum ← velocity  •  oversight → Where each school sits on the one axis that orders them.

The two poles trade off the same way: all velocity ships fast but leaves quality implicit; all oversight checks everything but makes checking the bottleneck. The midway keeps velocity and grows guardrails from the failures velocity surfaces.

read the full treatment →
The midway is a discipline Governance-centric — the synthesis Three process models for agentic engineering; this site takes the third.

Three process models for agentic engineering. The two poles: velocity-centric agents hand work around a ring of job titles with the quality mechanism left implicit; oversight-centric keeps a human next to each bounded piece — honest, but the human's attention does not scale with the fleet. Governance-centric is the synthesis: the agents sit inside a containing environment of enforced mechanisms the human sets up in advance. This site takes the third.

That midway means establishing and maintaining a governed engineering environment — working in two directions at once: up front you specify what you can (the architecture that makes a class of error impossible, the model the fleet reasons through, the templates that put a change on rails); in flight you let velocity surface the failures you couldn't foresee and convert each recurring one into a durable guardrail.

read the full treatment →
The Modeling Thesis — why a typed model beats prose
Modeling Thesis Agent-legible & precise Abstraction shrinks the space an agent can be wrong in.

A six-state machine with typed invariants is something an agent reasons over without error the way it cannot over 300,000 lines of prose-and-code. Abstraction shrinks the space it can be wrong in, not just the token count. A model is more precise than any document.

read the full treatment →
Modeling Thesis It can’t lie A model wired to a build-time drift check cannot rot.

A document rots the moment the code moves; a model wired to a build-time drift check cannot: the gate stays red until the map matches the territory again. That guarantee is what prose can never give — though a drift gate proves the model and code agree, not that either is right: the model must be authored, not merely read off the code, or a mirror of the bug passes green (2.2).

read the full treatment →
Modeling Thesis Cheap to keep, pays back Agents maintain the model like docs and tests.

Because agents build and maintain the model the way they maintain docs and tests, pointing them at it costs almost nothing, and it pays back in higher code quality, fewer tokens spent rederiving what the model already states, and fewer mistakes.

read the full treatment →
The Alignment Thesis — constraints and sensors
Alignment Thesis Constraint Make the wrong move impossible to pick.

Scope the agent's action space so the wrong move is never available to pick: the typed model, an enum instead of a free-form string, one sanctioned seam. A constraint prevents drift — the mistake costs no iteration, because the compiler rejects it on the spot. (Poka-yoke for software; building a constraint is what "architecture" does.)

read the full treatment →
Alignment Thesis Sensor Where you can't prevent it, detect it after the fact.

Where you can't prevent it, detect it after the fact: a lint, a gate, a validator, a test suite that fires on a violation and holds the line. A sensor detects drift and fails the loop iteration, so the agent runs again to fix what it caught. It costs iterations — which is why you don't reach for it first.

read the full treatment →
Alignment Thesis · validation Generate inputs to falsify a model Property tests, fuzzing, and fuzz+model are one move.

The strongest sensors don't check one example — they generate inputs and try to falsify a specification the model supplies. Property-based testing, fuzzing, and fuzzing driven by the typed model are one move at three richnesses of oracle: the model names the stable point in the spec, and the generator hunts a counterexample to it.

read the full treatment →
Constraint vs. sensor Firewall vs. smoke detector Prefer a constraint; wrap in sensors for what you can't scope away.

A sensor lets the mistake happen and catches it in time — a smoke detector. A constraint makes the whole class of mistake impossible — a firewall. Prefer a constraint where you can build one, because a sensor still spends an iteration. But a constraint across the only exit blocks the people trying to leave — an over-scoped design stops legitimate work as surely as the error, so add a sensor for the drift you cannot scope away. Most real mechanisms are a package across both: a soft constraint that aims the agent, wrapped in hard sensors that catch what it only aims at.

read the full treatment →
The residual Neither move reaches it Some goals have no sensor and no constraint — they stay a human job.

Not every goal splits into a constraint or a sensor. Some have neither — no cheap sensor can see the failure, no constraint can scope it away, because the failure is an absence nobody specified. A missing authorization check has no failing test by definition: a test that caught it would mean it was specified, and a specified check would not be missing. That goal stays a human job, and which of your goals land here sets your real throughput ceiling. This is not the soft end of a spectrum — a soft mechanism is still a mechanism; the residual has none. Naming it is the framework's honest edge: here is what the catalogue does not reach.

read the full treatment →
How the Alignment half grows Reading failure as a missing mechanism Velocity surfaces a failure class; you convert each recurring one into a mechanism.

You place some constraints and sensors up front, from what you know about the domain. The rest you learn along the way: velocity surfaces a failure class earlier governance didn't address, and you convert each recurring one into a mechanism. That conversion is the way of thinking inside MAGE — how the Alignment Thesis grows past what you could specify in advance.

1Velocity exposes failureAgent changes surface ambiguity, drift, and weak boundaries — fast.
→
2Monitoring intelligence classifies itLocal defect, or a recurring structural weakness?
→
3Convert to governanceEncode it: a type, a lint, a schema, a gate, or a harness rule.
→
4Action space narrowsEvery later agent inherits a smaller, more explicit space.

Governability compounds. The environment absorbs more agent work, so velocity stays sustainable.

Implementation is cheap; the judgment that decides which governance should exist is the costly, human part. Two paired concepts hold it together:

  • Governance makes velocity sustainable — guardrails are what let the fleet keep shipping fast without drowning in its own failures.
  • Judgment decides which governance to build — recognizing which failures deserve a guardrail (and which are one-offs) is the hard, human call.
read the full treatment →
What the engineer's job becomes
The engineer's job Models are the universal language of engineering Code was the bottleneck; now the model is the work.

For most of software's history the scarce resource was implementation — someone had to type the thing into existence, and that typing was the bottleneck everything queued behind. Agents moved that bottleneck: code is cheap to produce and fast to change, and a model wired to a drift check keeps the map in sync for free. What is not cheap is deciding what to build and authoring the model whose properties drive the tradeoffs. So the engineer's job relocates up — from producing code to authoring the models every other engineering discipline has always reasoned in, now finally cheap enough for software to speak too.

read the full treatment →
The engineer's job The judgment moved up, not away You're still accountable for the code an agent typed.

An engineer was always accountable for choices they did not hand-implement — the compiler they picked, the library, the algorithm. Delegating the keystrokes never delegated the accountability. The model level strips the accidental cost of holding a large system in a small window and leaves the essential difficulty in plain view, where judgment has to meet it. That essential residual does not yield to a tool — it moves one level up, from "write correct code" to "author the model that says what correct means."

read the full treatment →
The engineer's job Modelling democratizes The map used to be the architect's; now everyone can hold one.

Modelling used to be senior work — the one person who could hold the whole system in their head drew the map, and everyone else worked below it. Freed from the cost of typing and of keeping the map in sync by hand, every engineer can now reason about the system's properties and how their own change moves the whole. The map got cheap enough that everyone can hold one.

The way of thinking — three stances
Way of thinkingArchitect deliberatelybuy the right design; name shapes with types
  • Implementation is cheap; architecture compounds. Buy the right design, not the fast one.
  • Name shapes with types; primitive-passing leaves the architecture anonymous.
  • Make models, state, and policy explicit: state machines over scattered counters, enums over magic strings.
  • One canonical way beats many clever ones. Agents will apply patterns they see 200× with no debate.
  • Attack accidental complexity; budget for the essential kind.
read the full treatment →
Way of thinkingConvert failure into machineryencode each recurring failure as a lint, type, or gate
  • When a failure recurs, encode it (a lint, type, gate, or schema) instead of re-inspecting for it.
  • Move audits to lints: cheap, at-commit, deterministic beats expensive and post-hoc.
  • Let the compiler and gates hold the line; review is not a substitute for static analysis.
  • Never fail quiet: every caught error logs, re-throws, or is justified in a comment.
  • No compatibility shims. Migrate every call site in the same change.
read the full treatment →
Way of thinkingKeep judgment scarce & centralcarry work autonomously; spend human judgment where it counts
  • Carry work autonomously; surface only the architectural calls.
  • Hyper-experimentation: pilot, compare, measure; a cheap experiment beats a debate, and negative results are wins.
  • Verify claims and trust nothing stale. Re-run the gates yourself, because markers rot.
  • Reason about second-order dynamics: what happens at T+100, or under concurrency?
  • Documentation encodes invariants that drive tests, not prose that rots.
read the full treatment →
Way of thinking Where the stances come from Distilled from the AI-First Engineering Method.

Three stances that make the midway work, distilled from the AI-First Engineering Method (architecture, controls, and the stance that wields them); the full set ships in the starter CLAUDE.md.

The catalogue

A representative selection — mechanism patterns, not an exhaustive list of every lint and gate in the system. Each row is one mechanism with its one-line Summary and how it Enforces: Hard is deterministic (blocks, audits, or signals regardless of agent cooperation), Soft is probabilistic (aims an agent but cannot block), and Soft·Hard is soft guidance with a hard counterpart.
